4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 

I believe the song is **"Things We Said Today"** (from the 1964 album *A Hard Day's Night*).

The song is written in A minor, opening immediately on the tonic chord (**Am**) and jumping directly to the minor fifth chord, **Em** (the natural minor $v$ chord), on the lines *"You say you will love me / if I have to go..."* 

Rather than using the conventional major dominant ($V$ or $\text{E}^7$) common in traditional minor-key harmony, McCartney opts for the modal Aeolian/Dorian sound by moving straight from the tonic minor ($\text{i}$) to the minor fifth ($\text{v}$), creating that distinctive, somber oscillation right at the very beginning of the verse.

### Musicological and Harmonic Rationale

The Beatles song that definitively **"starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fifth chord"** is **"Things We Said Today"** (written by Paul McCartney, from the 1964 album *A Hard Day's Night*).

#### 1. A Literal, Unaccompanied Opening "Chord Jump" ($i \to v$)
* The track opens immediately on measure one, beat one, with Paul McCartney’s unaccompanied, percussive acoustic rhythm guitar.
* There are no vocal pickups, lead lines, or polyphonic studio textures obscuring the motion; the track establishes its core groove with an immediate, stark rhythmic leap from the tonic minor (**$\text{Am}$**, $\text{i}$) straight to the minor fifth chord (**$\text{Em}$**, $\text{v}$).
* This unadorned two-chord oscillation serves as the primary harmonic cell and rhythmic engine for the entire verse.

#### 2. Musicological Significance of "The Minor Fifth Chord"
* In classical functional harmony as well as standard pop songwriting in minor keys, the fifth scale degree is almost universally raised to a **major triad or dominant seventh** chord ($\text{V}$ or $\text{V}^7$, i.e., $\text{E}$ or $\text{E}^7$) to provide a leading-tone resolution ($G\sharp \to A$) back to the tonic.
* McCartney deliberately avoids the conventional major dominant pull, retaining the natural, unadorned minor fifth triad ($\text{Em}$, preserving the natural $G\natural$). As musicologists (such as Dominic Pedler in *The Songwriting Secrets of The Beatles*) observe, this immediate leap to the unraised minor fifth defines the song’s brooding, modal (Aeolian/Dorian) character right from the opening measure.

---

However, contrapuntal analyses (such as Alan W. Pollack’s) emphasize that the iconic Mellotron intro is governed by polyphonic, stepwise descending chromatic inner voice-leading ($A \to G\sharp \to G\natural \to F\sharp$) and passing inversions rather than an isolated, rhythmic block "chord jump."
* **"Any Time At All" (Key: D major):** Starts directly on beat one with vocals, leaping from the major tonic (**$\text{D}$**, $\text{I}$) on *"Any time at all..."* to the minor fifth (**$\text{Am}$**, $\text{v}$) on *"...any time at all"*, though this operates as a rapid vocal phrase within a broader chorus progression ($D \to Am \to C \to D$).

---

### Conclusion

Because **"Things We Said Today"** literally opens on beat one with an unaccompanied, definitive rhythm guitar jump from the tonic directly to the natural minor fifth chord ($\text{Am} \to \text{Em}$), it remains the most direct, accurate, and structurally complete answer to the question.
